# Nonallergic rhinitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric ENT and pulmonology > Nonallergic rhinitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/vj0AXT)

---

## Summary

Nonallergic <u>rhinitis</u> (NAR) is an acute or chronic <u>rhinitis</u> that is not immune mediated. There are several <u>types of NAR</u>, including infectious <u>rhinitis</u>, <u>nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome</u>, <u>vasomotor rhinitis</u> (<u>VMR</u>), <u>drug-induced rhinitis</u>, and <u>atrophic rhinitis</u>. <u>Common clinical features of NAR</u> are persistent or intermittent nasal congestion, <u>postnasal drip</u>, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, and sneezing. Diagnosis is usually clinical; <u>allergen testing</u> is not routinely recommended. Management includes avoidance of triggers and topical pharmacological treatment with intranasal <u>antihistamines</u> (INAH) and/or intranasal <u>corticosteroids</u> (INCS). Additional therapies (e.g., intranasal <u>ipratropium</u>, intranasal decongestants) are considered for certain <u>types of NAR</u>. Refractory or severe symptoms require specialist referral for advanced treatments (e.g., oral medications, <u>surgery</u>).




Infectious <u>rhinitis</u> often occurs in conjunction with <u>sinusitis</u> (<u>infectious rhinosinusitis</u>); see “<u>Sinusitis</u>” for details. <u>Allergic rhinitis</u> is a distinct entity and is detailed separately.

| <br><u>Vasomotor rhinitis</u> (<u>VMR</u>) | <br>* <u>Rhinitis</u> caused by an increase in blood flow to the nasal <u>mucosa</u> usually in response to triggers<br><br> | <br><br>* Often <u>idiopathic</u><br><br>* Irritant odors (e.g., <u>cigarette smoke</u>, perfumes) [[2]](/library/kIdm1r0)<br><br>* Cold and/or dry air<br><br>* Changes in <u>humidity</u><br><br>* Exercise<br><br>* Foods (e.g., hot temperature, spicy)<br><br>* <u>Alcohol</u><br><br><br> |
| Rhinitis in older adults | <br>* Chronic watery <u>rhinorrhea</u> in older individuals<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Age-related changes</u> (e.g., <u>mucosal</u> <u>atrophy</u>, decreased blood flow)<br><br>* May be triggered by irritants (e.g., certain foods, odors)<br><br>* <u>Drug-induced rhinitis</u> is common in older individuals.<br><br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

* Nasal congestion, mouth breathing, snoring, and/or <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Rhinorrhea</u>, <u>postnasal drip</u>, throat clearing, <u>cough</u>

* Sneezing

* Possible <u>anosmia</u>, <u>eustachian tube dysfunction</u>

* <u>Headache</u>, sinus pressure

* <u>Allergic shiners</u> may be present.

* See “<u>Types of NAR</u>” for findings according to subtypes.





> [!NOTE]
> Nonallergic and <u>allergic rhinitis</u> often manifest with similar symptoms (e.g., <u>rhinorrhea</u>, sneezing, mouth breathing), but <u>postnasal drip</u> is more common in NAR, and <u>pruritus</u> of the mouth, nose, and <u>ear</u> are more common in <u>allergic rhinitis</u>. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Vasomotor rhinitis (<u>idiopathic rhinitis</u>) [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)[[3]](/library/yqddar0)




A type of NAR that is caused by an increase in blood flow to the nasal <u>mucosa</u>, usually in response to an irritant or stimulant [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)




#### Etiology




* Irritant odors;  (e.g., <u>cigarette smoke</u>, perfumes)

* Cold and/or dry air

* Changes in <u>humidity</u>, temperature, and air pressures

* Exercise

* Foods (e.g., hot temperature, spicy)

* <u>Alcohol</u>





#### Pathophysiology [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)




* ↑ <u>Parasympathetic</u> activity: <u>Parasympathetic</u> stimulation causes vasodilatation of <u>blood vessels</u> in the nasal <u>mucosa</u> and increases mucous secretion.

* ↓ <u>Sympathetic</u> activity: <u>Sympathetic</u> stimulation causes <u>vasoconstriction</u> of the nasal <u>blood vessels</u>.





#### Clinical features




* Clear nasal discharge

* Nasal congestion

* <u>Cough</u>

* Sneezing and itching are typically absent.

* See also “<u>Common clinical features of NAR</u>.”





#### Management




* Diagnosis is clinical; see “<u>Diagnosis of NAR</u>.”

* Initial treatment of VMR [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

* Avoid triggers, if feasible.

* Start monotherapy with INAH or INCS.

* Persistent symptoms: Add or switch to intranasal <u>ipratropium</u> to control <u>anterior</u> <u>rhinorrhea</u>.

* Severe or refractory symptoms: Endoscopic <u>vidian neurectomy</u> may be considered.  [[5]](/library/wIdhUr0)

* See “<u>Treatment of NAR</u>” for details and dosages.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Vasomotor rhinitis</u> is a diagnosis of exclusion. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)




### Atrophic rhinitis [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)[[6]](/library/9IdNUr0)




A chronic condition in which nasal crusting and dry <u>mucosa</u> are associated with <u>atrophy</u> of the nasal <u>mucosa</u>




#### Etiology




* Primary <u>atrophic rhinitis</u>

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Often associated with bacterial <u>colonization</u> (<u>K. pneumoniae</u> subsp. ozaenae is most common)

* More common in individuals residing in resource-limited settings with a dry climate

* Secondary <u>atrophic rhinitis</u>

* Trauma (e.g., repeated <u>surgery</u>, <u>radiotherapy</u>) involving the nasal <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Granulomatous diseases</u> of the nasal cavity (e.g., <u>syphilis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>leprosy</u>)





#### Clinical features




* Foul-smelling nasal cavity with or without <u>anosmia</u>

* Nasal dryness and crusting

* <u>Epistaxis</u>

* <u>Empty nose syndrome</u> (in secondary <u>atrophic rhinitis</u>)





#### Diagnosis




* Diagnosis is clinical.

* In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, consider:

* <u>Bacterial culture</u> of the nasal <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u> of the nasal <u>mucosa</u>

* Evaluation for suspected underlying systemic conditions, e.g.:

* <u>Diagnostics for sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for syphilis</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for leprosy</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for tuberculosis</u>

* See also “<u>Diagnosis of NAR</u>.”





#### Treatment




<u>Atrophic rhinitis</u> is managed differently from other <u>types of NAR</u>. Refer to an ENT specialist for management.




* <u>Conservative management</u> options to reduce nasal crusting include:

* Nasal saline <u>irrigation</u>

* Glycerin drops

* <u>Emollients</u>

* <u>Antibiotics</u> targeting specific pathogens

* Nasal <u>estradiol</u>

* Surgical options to decrease the volume of the nasal cavity: e.g., modified Young procedure, prostheses  [[6]](/library/9IdNUr0)

---

## Diagnosis

* NAR is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* Perform a <u>physical examination</u>, including:

* Focused <u>head and neck examination</u> (e.g., <u>otoscopy</u>, <u>nasal inspection</u> with <u>anterior rhinoscopy</u>)

* <u>Skin examination</u>: to evaluate for signs of <u>atopy</u> and/or systemic disease

* In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, consider additional diagnostic studies and/or referral to a specialist (e.g., ENT) for: [[3]](/library/yqddar0)

* <u>Diagnostics for allergic rhinitis</u>

* Imaging for suspected <u>sinusitis</u>, <u>nasal polyps</u>, or <u>nasopharyngeal cancer</u>

* <u>Nasopharyngoscopy</u> to evaluate for structural abnormalities and/or complications





> [!TIP]
> For patients with significant <u>edema</u> of the nasal <u>mucosa</u>, consider using an intranasal decongestant before the examination to improve visibility. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

---

## Treatment

* There is no standard treatment algorithm for the <u>management of NAR</u>. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

* The following approach primarily applies to nonpregnant patients. Consult relevant specialists to determine the safety of <u>pharmacological treatment during pregnancy</u>. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)[[3]](/library/yqddar0)

* Treatment of <u>atrophic rhinitis</u> and <u>infectious rhinosinusitis</u> are detailed separately.





### First-line treatment




* Avoid triggers when possible; see “<u>Types of NAR</u>.”

* Start monotherapy with either of the following:

* Intranasal <u>antihistamines</u> (INAH): <u>azelastine</u> (<u>off-label</u> except for <u>VMR</u>) DOSAGE

* Intranasal <u>corticosteroids</u> (INCS): <u>fluticasone</u> DOSAGEor <u>beclomethasone</u> (<u>off-label</u> except for <u>VMR</u>) DOSAGE

* Consider adding the following:

* Intranasal saline as needed for symptom control  [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

* Intranasal decongestants for ≤ 5 days for severe symptoms or <u>mucosal</u> <u>edema</u> 

* <u>Oxymetazoline</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* <u>Phenylephrine</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE





### Further management




Reassess patients 5–7 days after starting monotherapy.




#### Symptom improvement




* Triggers are controlled or absent: Stop or taper off treatment.

* Triggers cannot be controlled: Continue treatment as needed (<u>PRN</u>).





#### Persistent symptoms




* Consider alternative monotherapy (preferred).

* Add or switch to a symptom-specific agent.

* Predominant <u>anterior</u> <u>rhinorrhea</u> (e.g., <u>VMR</u>, <u>gustatory rhinitis</u>, <u>rhinitis in older adults</u>): intranasal <u>ipratropium</u> DOSAGE[[1]](/library/WlXPDy)[[2]](/library/kIdm1r0)

* Predominant nasal congestion: intranasal decongestant for ≤ 5 days; see “First-line treatment” for dosages.





#### Severe symptoms or symptoms refractory to monotherapy  [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)




* Consider combination intranasal therapy of INAH + INCS; see “First-line treatment” for dosages.  [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)

* Refer to ENT for oral pharmacotherapy options and/or <u>surgery</u> (e.g.,<u>vidian neurectomy</u> for <u>VMR</u>, <u>turbinectomy</u>).





> [!WARNING]
> Oral <u>antihistamines</u> and <u>leukotriene-receptor antagonists</u> are not recommended because of insufficient evidence on their <u>efficacy</u>. [[1]](/library/WlXPDy)
